answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources include /databases, /collections, etc.). Example ARM/Bicep resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name my-docdb-account --resource-group rg --locations regionName='West US' --kind MongoDB --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'acct' ... }). Terraform (AzureRM): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "acct" location = "West US" offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... } (and Terraform has azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DB/collection child resources).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
MongoDB-style URI. Example concrete form used by apps: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@
Notes: username is often specified as '<dbuser>@<account>' for Cosmos Mongo API; host suffix is .mongo.cosmos.azure.com; TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true). Default TLS MongoDB port on Cosmos is 10255 (plaintext 10255 with TLS required); common query options: replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, appName set to identify client.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB API for MongoDB) is billed by Request Units (RUs) when using provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is also a serverless option for small, intermittent workloads. In short: primary billing unit is RUs (with autoscale or manual RU/s); there is not a simple vCore-based SKU in the classic Cosmos DB account billing model.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with username/password (SCRAM) where the account user is mapped to the Cosmos account; commonly the password is an access key (primary/key). Cosmos DB SQL API also supports master keys and resource tokens. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not a supported auth mechanism for the MongoDB wire protocol in Cosmos (i.e. you cannot directly use AAD OAuth token in a standard MongoDB driver for Cosmos); instead use username/password (or service principal to obtain keys out-of-band).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. Python: pymongo or motor for async). There is a separate Azure SDK for Cosmos DB (azure-cosmos) but for applications talking to the MongoDB API you should use the MongoDB driver (pymongo) because it speaks the MongoDB wire protocol. No separate 'mongodb-for-azure' driver is required.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Assuming the managed MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB supports vector indexes, create them using a MongoDB-style createIndex with a 'vector' index spec. Example (commit as-is): db.patients.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "emb_vec_hnsw", vector: { algorithm: "hnsw", similarity: "cosine", dims: 1536 } }) — specifying algorithm: "hnsw" (other supported algorithms might include ivf or diskann). (I am uncertain about exact option names and driver support.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB/Mongo API does not embed a full-featured text search engine like MongoDB Atlas Search. For full-text or hybrid (text + vector) search you typically integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (pushing documents via change feed or ETL) or use an external search engine. There is no built-in Atlas-style hybrid search unless the managed service explicitly exposes a 'search' index—plan to use Azure Cognitive Search or an external search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API historically lags upstream MongoDB versions; it supports a particular MongoDB wire protocol version (examples: 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 in different account SKUs). Expect some features to be missing: server-side JS in the shell, some aggregation stages/operators, multi-document ACID transactions across shards/collections may be limited, and some admin commands are not supported. Confirm the account's selected 'server version' when creating the account. (I would check the account for the exact supported version before coding.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB emulator for local development. Docker image: mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator (run according to Microsoft docs). The emulator exposes the Cosmos endpoints (SQL, etc.) and typically listens on standard emulator ports (e.g. 8081 for the SQL endpoint); for the MongoDB protocol the cloud service uses port 10255/TLS, but the emulator historically had limited API support and may not expose the MongoDB API. If you need an identical Mongo wire-protocol experience locally, run an official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) for functional tests on the Mongo protocol. Ports: MongoDB default 27017 for local mongo image; Cosmos cloud Mongo endpoint uses 10255 with TLS.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a change feed feature on its core engine (SQL API). The MongoDB changeStreams API (as exposed by MongoDB drivers) may not be fully supported on the Cosmos Mongo API; use the Cosmos DB change feed for reliable change capture. If using the Cosmos change feed you must enable/consume it (it's available by default on containers/partitions) — no extra toggles beyond provisioning the container, but SDKs differ. If you want driver-compatible MongoDB change streams, expect them not to be available or limited.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: There is a service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' referenced in the run environment; use the 'documentdb' MCP server's tools for data-plane inspection. The general Azure MCP server covers many Azure services, but for fine-grained DocumentDB/Cosmos DB data-plane operations the 'documentdb' MCP server provides the specialized tools and inspection commands.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically the service was called DocumentDB and was later rebranded/expanded into Azure Cosmos DB. The name DocumentDB refers to Microsoft's original JSON-document database; Azure Cosmos DB is the globally distributed multi-model service that superseded it. This Microsoft 'DocumentDB' is not the same as any separate open-source 'DocumentDB' project—Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed service that provides MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility via an API surface.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/engine with a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol on top; in other words it is not running the upstream MongoDB server internally. That means most MongoDB drivers and queries will work, but some server-side behaviors, unsupported commands, performance characteristics, and consistency/transaction semantics may differ — test queries and aggregation pipelines. Application code primarily uses standard MongoDB drivers but must avoid unsupported server features.

answers.question: How will the sample connect to the cluster at runtime (connection string mechanics and code)?
answers.answer:
Read the URI from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it unchanged to pymongo.MongoClient. Example Python: from pymongo import MongoClient
client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=False)
Use the options already present in the URI (ssl=true or tls=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false). Never hard-code the URI; use a .env.example with a placeholder.

answers.question: What collection and TTL cache structure will the sample create for materialised aggregation caches?
answers.answer: Create a collection named aggregations_cache in database sample_healthcare_16. Documents will be { _id: '<aggregation_key>', result: <materialized_result>, lastUpdated: ISODate(...), ttl: ISODate(...) }. Create a TTL index on field 'ttl' with expireAfterSeconds: 0: db.aggregations_cache.createIndex({ ttl: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 }). Use this collection to store cached aggregation results and allow automatic expiry.

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will be used for the faceted dashboard endpoints?
answers.answer:
Use a $facet stage to produce multiple summaries in one query. Example pipeline (pymongo syntax): pipeline = [ { '$match': match_filter }, { '$facet': { 'byDiagnosis': [ { '$sortByCount': '$diagnosis' } ], 'byAgeBand': [ { '$bucket': { 'groupBy': '$age', 'boundaries': [0,18,35,50,65,200], 'default': 'unknown' } } ], 'byGender': [ { '$sortByCount': '$gender' } ], 'byRegion': [ { '$sortByCount': '$region' } ] } } ]
Run db.patients.aggregate(pipeline). This single aggregation returns all facets in one round-trip for dashboards.

answers.question: Which indexes should the sample create to make the dashboard aggregations efficient?
answers.answer: Create single-field indexes on the fields used in matching and faceting: db.patients.createIndex({ diagnosis: 1 }); db.patients.createIndex({ age: 1 }); db.patients.createIndex({ gender: 1 }); db.patients.createIndex({ region: 1 }); For common cohort queries that combine filters, create compound indexes matching the common filter shapes, e.g. db.patients.createIndex({ region: 1, age: 1, diagnosis: 1 }). Also create the TTL index for the cache collection as described.

answers.question: Which client libraries and packages will the sample use and how are they installed?
answers.answer: Use Python with pymongo for DB access and FastAPI for the web framework. Install with pip: pip install fastapi uvicorn pymongo python-dotenv. For async endpoints you may use motor (pip install motor) instead of pymongo. Use python-dotenv in development to load DOCUMENTDB_URI from .env.
